question.explain: False. An ideal type is a deliberately one-sided analytical construct; it is not found in reality as such, and its value is tested by adequacy. ‘Ideal’ means ‘constructed in thought’, not ‘best’.

quiz.prompt: Which thinker coined the word “sociology”, and in which work and year does it appear?
options: Durkheim, *The Rules of Sociological Method*, 1895
Spencer, *Principles of Sociology*, 1876
Comte, *Cours de philosophie positive*, fourth volume, 1839
Weber, *Economy and Society*, 1921
quiz.explain: The word is presented as a new term in a footnote in the 1839 fourth volume of Comte’s *Cours*. Durkheim and Weber belong to the generation after Comte and did not coin the word; Spencer is not its creator either, but the creator of the phrase ‘survival of the fittest’.

quiz.prompt: True or false: In *Suicide* Durkheim argued that suicide never spreads from individual to individual.
quiz.explain: False. Durkheim writes that he is sure suicide is contagious from individual to individual; in his view imitation is not strong enough to determine the social suicide rate. Separating the two claims is the key both in exams and in the newspaper–suicide debate.

quiz.prompt: Match each thinker with the concept he is most associated with.
pairs: The stranger and the blasé attitude
quiz.explain: The pair most often confused is Durkheim–Weber: both wrote about ‘authority/legitimacy’ and ‘social order’, but anomie and the social fact are Durkheim’s concepts, the ideal type and Verstehen Weber’s. Wesenwille–Kürwille are Tönnies’s two kinds of will; Simmel’s stranger and blasé attitude come from his metropolis writings.

quiz.prompt: Put the following events in chronological order (earliest to latest).
items: Comte: the fourth volume containing the word “sociologie” (1839)
Weber: the proposal of a press survey at the German Sociological Society (1910)
Shils and Young: the meaning of the coronation (1953)
quiz.explain: The order is 1839, 1887, 1897, 1903, 1910, 1953. It helps to remember that Tönnies came before Durkheim and Simmel (1887): he is the oldest of this generation. Weber’s press proposal is seven years after Simmel’s metropolis essay.

quiz.text: For Durkheim, weak integration gives rise to {{1}} suicide and weak regulation to {{2}} suicide; the fourth type, {{3}} suicide, does not appear in the main text and is mentioned only in a footnote.

options: altruistic
egoistic
anomic
egoistic
altruistic
anomic
altruistic
fatalistic
egoistic

quiz.explain: Egoistic suicide arises from weak integration and anomic suicide from weak regulation; fatalistic suicide arises from excessive regulation and appears in *Suicide* only in a footnote. Altruistic suicide is one of the three main types but is related not to weak integration but to excessive immersion.

quiz.scenario: Imagine a public broadcaster airs live all day on a national day of mourning; the streets are empty, people watch together at home. Two researchers interpret the broadcast separately.

parts.prompt: The first researcher says “The broadcast reaffirms a shared value and integrates society.” Which classical strand is this reading closest to?
options: Durkheim’s ritual and integration reading
Weber’s Verstehen
Simmel’s figure of the stranger
parts.explain: The reaffirmation of shared values and social integration is the central idea of the Durkheim line (and of Shils and Young’s 1953 reading). Weber’s Verstehen deals with the meaning of individual action, Simmel’s stranger with the figure of nearness and distance; integration is not their main question.

parts.prompt: The second researcher says “Integration is too simple a notion; we should look at whom the broadcast leaves out and which interest it brings forward.” Whom does this objection resemble most?
options: Comte’s law of three stages
Criticisms of the Birnbaum (1955) and Lukes (1975) kind
Tönnies’s Wesenwille
parts.explain: Birnbaum argued that divergence and tension are normal; Lukes argued that neo-Durkheimian readings use integration too simply. Comte’s law of three stages and Tönnies’s Wesenwille are not part of this debate.

parts.prompt: What is the most sensible first step in testing both claims?
options: Looking only at the audience figures
Looking at which of the two researchers is more famous
Recording together what events the broadcast covers and how, and what meaning the audience attaches to it
parts.explain: Weber’s 1910 plan proposed first a quantitative measurement of content and then qualitative analysis; ‘Verstehen’ requires taking into account the meaning attached by the audience as well. Audience figures alone show neither integration nor bias; fame is not evidence.

quiz.takeaway: The same broadcast is open to both an integration and an interest/power reading; both have to be tested together with content and audience data.

quiz.prompt: What does the footnote in the 1947 Henderson–Parsons translation say about Weber’s word *Herrschaft*?
options: That it should always be translated as ‘sovereignty’.
That it has no satisfactory English equivalent; ‘imperative control’ serves for general use and ‘authority’ where it is legitimate.
That it means only ‘power’.
That it cannot be translated and must never be rendered into English.
quiz.explain: The footnote says that the word has no satisfactory English equivalent, that they borrowed the term ‘imperative control’ for general use, and that for legitimate *Herrschaft* ‘authority’ is both accurate and less awkward. ‘Power’ is kept for *Macht*, not for *Herrschaft*.

quiz.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of Weber’s three types of legitimate domination (authority)?
options: Traditional
Charismatic
Legal-rational
Mechanical
quiz.explain: Weber’s triad is traditional, charismatic and legal-rational. ‘Mechanical’ comes from Durkheim’s concept of mechanical solidarity; in exams two names and two triads are often confused.

quiz.scenario: Imagine Arda has just moved to a large city. In the mornings he sees hundreds of faces but speaks to no one. One night, on an anonymous forum, he writes to strangers something he has told nobody.

parts.prompt: According to Simmel’s 1903 essay, which concept best describes the city dweller’s attitude towards the crowd?
options: Mechanical solidarity
Charismatic domination
The reserved attitude (Reserviertheit)
parts.explain: Simmel writes that if the city dweller tried to respond inwardly to countless people he would split apart psychologically, so he develops a reserved attitude. Mechanical solidarity and charismatic domination are concepts of other thinkers.

parts.prompt: How can Arda’s anonymous confession be related to Simmel’s 1908 figure of the ‘stranger’?
options: Simmel measured an increase in confession on online forums.
Simmel said that confession is never made to a stranger.

Simmel writes that confessions withheld from those close to us are sometimes made to the stranger, especially the one passing through; this reading extended to the online setting is an interpretation.
parts.explain: Simmel’s text records that to the stranger (especially the one passing through) openness is shown that is withheld from those close; the online setting did not exist in Simmel’s time, so the link is an interpretation.

parts.prompt: What is the status of this link?
options: A documented finding of Simmel’s
An interpretation; not Simmel’s finding
A law of Tönnies’s
parts.explain: Simmel wrote about neither the online setting nor forums; this reading is our interpretation. A ‘law’ appears nowhere in this lesson; Tönnies’s ideal types are not laws either.

quiz.takeaway: Extending a classical concept to a present-day situation can be useful, but one should say that it is an interpretation.

quiz.prompt: Which of the following is true according to the abstract of Phillips’s (1974) article?
options: The stories had no effect on suicides.
The rise was seen evenly across the country, unrelated to where the story was published.
In Britain and the United States between 1947 and 1968, suicides rose immediately after suicide stories published in newspapers; the more space given to the story, the larger the rise.
The study recalculated Durkheim’s 1897 data.
quiz.explain: The abstract reports a rise immediately after the story, a larger rise after stories given more space, and a rise largely confined to the area where the story was published. The first and second options say the opposite; the fourth confuses Phillips’s data with Durkheim’s.

quiz.prompt: Which is the correct interpretation of Durkheim’s rule “treat social facts as things”?
options: Using people like objects.
Treating social facts as data given to observation, independently of personal opinions.
Holding that social facts are physical objects.
Ignoring the individual’s inner world.
quiz.explain: Durkheim’s text defines a ‘thing’ as whatever is given to observation and imposes itself on it, and equates treating facts as things with treating them as the starting data of science. The first and third options read a concept whose name is ‘thing’ literally; the fourth rests on the cliché that Durkheim ignored the individual.

quiz.prompt: True or false: The press survey Weber proposed in 1910 was completed and became the German Sociological Society’s first big publication.
quiz.explain: False. In 1912 Weber said that the enterprise had suffered a “very special ill fortune”; according to Lepsius he abandoned the project in 1911. The plan therefore went down in history as a research programme that was never carried out.
